extracted.intended_audience: regulatory analysts, immigration lawyers, benefits-administering agencies, nonprofit advocates, and affected noncitizens
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory economic analysis and cost–benefit accounting for a DHS final rule on the public charge ground of inadmissibility, including form time burdens, opportunity costs, transfer payments, baseline selection, and alternative scenarios. Intended to support rulemaking and public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time burden components for form filings
rubrics_metrics.description: The time burden estimate includes the time for reviewing instructions, gathering the required documentation and information, completing the affidavit/application, preparing statements, attaching necessary documentation, and submitting the affidavit/application/request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to multiple forms (e.g., Form I-864EZ: 2.5 hours; Form I-864W: 1 hour; Form I-485 baseline 6.42 hours increased to 7.17 hours under final rule). The estimate is explicit about the constituent tasks that compose 'time burden.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity cost of time using average total rate of compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute opportunity cost of time for completing and submitting forms by multiplying time burden by an average total rate of compensation (example rate used: $39.55/hour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Form I-864EZ 2.5 hours × $39.55 = $98.88; Form I-864W 1 hour × $39.55 = $39.55. DHS uses this method as the standard for monetizing time burdens for many populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of minimum-wage-based rate for certain populations
rubrics_metrics.description: For some populations not likely participating in the labor market, use a total rate based on minimum wage plus weighted average benefits (example used: $17.11/hour) to estimate opportunity cost of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS used $17.11/hour when estimating opportunity costs for the population filing Form I-485 who are subject to the public charge ground, and for small populations like T nonimmigrant I-601 filers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate additional time burden from new regulatory questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify increases in form-completion time due to added instructions and questions required by the final rule (e.g., additional 0.75 hours for Form I-485 to collect information on age, health, family status, assets/resources/financial status, education and skills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS explains changes in instrument design (open-ended narrative questions changed to multiple-choice) that affect time; it reports the net revised time (Form I-485 final time 7.17 hours, reflecting a 0.75 hour increase). Use these deltas to compute new annual costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include filing fees in cost/savings calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Include statutory/administrative filing fees as part of total costs or savings when relevant (e.g., filing fee for Form I-601 = $930 is included in computing savings when waiver filing is no longer required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS combines fee totals with opportunity cost of time to produce aggregate annual savings (example: 16 filers × $930 = $14,880; plus time cost yields ~$15,359 annual savings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarization cost estimation method
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate 'familiarization costs' as opportunity cost of the time spent reading and reviewing the rule, using an assumed reading time and wage rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS assumes ~8–9 hours per person to read the rule, reading speed of 250–300 words per minute, and uses $39.55/hour average total compensation to estimate per-person costs of ~$316.40 to $355.95, but notes inability to estimate the number of readers and thus cannot quantify total familiarization cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply standard discount rates for multi-year comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply 3 percent and 7 percent discount rates to total estimated costs and savings to compare costs over time and present 10-year discounted net costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS reports undiscounted 10‑year totals and also presents discounted net costs at both 3% and 7% (e.g., 10-year undiscounted direct costs ~$64.36M; discounted net costs ~$54.77M at 3% and ~$45.09M at 7%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat transfer payments as transfers, not net resource changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify changes in Federal/State transfer payments separately and recognize that transfers are monetary movements between groups that do not change total resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS distinguishes direct costs from transfer payment changes (e.g., estimated annual transfer payment decreases/increases under alternatives) and notes these are transfers and broader in consequence than direct regulatory costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a Pre-Guidance (pre-statutory) baseline per OMB Circular A-4
rubrics_metrics.description: When substantial portions of a rule may restate statutory requirements, include a 'pre-guidance' baseline (a state of the world without prior guidance) in addition to the No Action baseline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS uses a Pre-Guidance baseline (i.e., state before the 1999 Interim Field Guidance) to provide additional perspective on long-run impacts and to comply with OMB Circular A-4 guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use literature and historical evidence to assess 'chilling effects' and disenrollment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess and discuss the potential chilling effect (reduced participation in public benefits) using historical studies and empirical literature when estimating indirect impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS cites studies (e.g., USDA study on food stamp declines 1994–1997, other analyses showing larger declines among noncitizens) and uses these to inform qualitative and quantitative discussion of likely disenrollment and downstream public health/economic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project populations using historical filing data
rubrics_metrics.description: Project future populations (e.g., number of filers affected) by using historical filing data over selected fiscal years and averaging as the basis for projections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: DHS uses FY2014–FY2018 Form I-601 historical filings for T nonimmigrants (average annual filers = 16) to project future reduced filings over a 10-year period beginning FY2022.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude benefits received during exempt immigration categories from public charge consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not consider public benefits that were received while a noncitizen was present in an immigration category that is exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility, including certain resettlement assistance and benefits for unaccompanied alien children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states these exclusions explicitly as policy clarifications intended to avoid penalizing benefit receipt in exempt statuses and to potentially increase participation among certain groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not count benefit receipt on behalf of another as the noncitizen's receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying for or obtaining public benefits on one's own behalf or on behalf of another does not constitute receipt of public benefits by the noncitizen for public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarification means assistance received solely on behalf of another individual (or if the noncitizen assisted with another's application) will not be treated as receipt by the noncitizen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare regulatory alternatives using additive effects and qualitative discussion when unquantifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating an alternative rule, sum effects relative to Pre-Guidance baseline and No Action baseline and provide quantitative estimates where possible and qualitative description where not quantifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS evaluated an Alternative similar to the 2018 NPRM/2019 Final Rule by updating prior estimates and combining effects; where impacts could not be reliably quantified, DHS supplies qualitative discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate disenrollment/forgone enrollment rate by ratio of adjustors to noncitizen population (example: 2.5%)
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate the share of public benefits recipients likely to disenroll or forgo enrollment, use the five-year average annual number of persons adjusting status divided by the estimated noncitizen population (DHS used this method to estimate 2.5%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS acknowledges this approach may tend toward overestimation (assumes 100% of such noncitizens and household members are enrolled or eligible and sufficiently concerned to disenroll) and may also understate broader chilling effects outside the adjustment population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute USCIS adjudication costs to fees and account for potential future fee adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS establishes fees to recover adjudication and administrative costs; the fee associated with I-485 is used to capture costs of other forms that currently have no fee, and future fee schedule adjustments may be necessary to recover additional operating costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS estimates increased USCIS employee costs from additional adjudication time (example: ~$14 million per year) and notes that fee setting will be addressed in the biennial fee review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and disclose inability to quantify some indirect and administrative impacts due to data limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where reliable data are lacking—e.g., number of people who will familiarize themselves with the rule, marginal administrative costs per enrollee for states—explicitly note inability to quantify impacts and avoid unsupported numeric estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS provides qualitative discussion of possible indirect effects (e.g., increased state administrative costs, downstream public health effects) but repeatedly documents data gaps that prevent quantification.
